pairs.rationale: The preceding conclusion about all these receiving testimony through faith and not being perfected apart from us supplies the argument's immediate background for therefore and the cloud of witnesses. The connection carries forward their faith examples without asserting that every earlier person is literally watching the readers' race.

Both depict purposeful running through an athletic race image. Corinthians names runners, self-control and the contrast between their perishable wreath and our imperishable one; Hebrews names endurance and laying aside weight and entangling sin. The image does not imply that only one believer receives the promised good.

Both join Christ's endurance of death on a cross with exaltation. Philippians names obedience and God highly exalting Him; Hebrews names the joy set before Jesus, the despised shame and His session at God's right hand. The pioneer/perfecter and enthronement details are not inserted into Philippians.

The preceding named Jesus, who endured a cross and its shame, supplies the One the readers are to consider. The appeal develops that model through opposition from sinners and the purpose of avoiding weariness. This is an internal example-and-exhortation link, not a second report of the suffering.

The earlier witnesses include people flogged, imprisoned, stoned and killed by the sword. Their severe suffering provides an internal contrast with these readers not yet resisting to blood in their struggle against sin. It does not identify a particular reader's injury or define every form of that struggle.

The son-address and warning not to make light of the Lord's discipline correspond to Proverbs. Proverbs says lose heart when corrected, while Hebrews says faint when reproved and presents the saying as encouragement to sons. The actual formulations are retained.

Both say that the Lord disciplines the one He loves and scourges every son He receives. Hebrews continues the cited encouragement in its endurance argument; Proverbs places the saying in instruction about receiving the Lord's correction. No different edition's wording is substituted.

Both compare the Lord's discipline with a father disciplining his son. Deuteronomy tells Israel to recognize the analogy in its heart; Hebrews commands endurance and reasons from ordinary father/son discipline to God dealing with the readers as sons. The audiences and immediate applications differ.

The preceding question about a father's disciplining his son gives the explicit premise for the following if-without-discipline inference. The letter itself develops the sonship contrast; the connection does not add an external legal definition of illegitimacy or identify an unprinted person as excluded.

The prayer in Numbers addresses God as God of the spirits and of all flesh; Hebrews contrasts fathers in the flesh with the Father of spirits. The uncommon spirits/flesh divine-relation language is shared, while the titles, prayer context and submission-and-life appeal remain distinct.

Both connect the readers' holiness with God's holiness. Peter calls people to holy conduct according to the Holy One who called them; Hebrews describes God's beneficial discipline so they may share His holiness, contrasted with the human fathers' limited discipline. The specific means and formulations differ.

Both bring righteousness's fruit together with peace. James describes its sowing in peace for peacemakers; Hebrews describes discipline's later peaceful fruit for those trained through it, despite present sorrow. The sowing and training processes are not made identical.

The paired hands-and-knees exhortation corresponds to Isaiah's limp hands and paralyzed knees. Isaiah says be strong; Hebrews says straighten the drooping hands and weakened knees in its discipline-and-endurance appeal. The bodily expressions retain their different wording.

The make-straight-tracks-for-your-feet wording is printed in Proverbs. Hebrews adds the purpose that what is lame be healed rather than dislocated; Proverbs adds directing ways rightly and avoiding an evil way. Neither passage receives the other's additional clause as its own wording.

Both urge peace with all people. Romans qualifies the appeal by what is possible and depends on the readers; Hebrews says pursue peace with everyone and also names sanctification and seeing the Lord. The latter holiness statement is not supplied as Romans' wording.

The root springing up in gall and bitterness in Deuteronomy corresponds to Hebrews' growing root of bitterness. Deuteronomy describes a person or group turning from the Lord to other gods; Hebrews warns of falling short of grace, trouble and defilement of many. The images and consequences remain in their own settings.

Genesis narrates Esau selling his birthright to Jacob in exchange for bread and lentil stew, then says he despised it. Hebrews uses that specific birthright-for-a-meal act in its warning about being profane like Esau. Genesis is not represented as narrating a sexual offense in this episode.

Genesis records Esau pleading for a blessing after his brother had taken it, then lifting his voice and weeping. This supplies the named blessing-and-tears background for Hebrews' rejected request. The reference does not decide the precise referent of it or give a complete interpretation of no place for repentance, nor assert that Genesis grants him no further blessing of any kind.

Exodus names Sinai's dark cloud, thunder, lightning, smoke and God's descent in fire, with the people brought beneath the mountain. This is the concrete earlier mountain scene set beside Hebrews' not-approached tangible fire, gloom and storm, before its Zion contrast. The recipients are not said to have physically stood at ancient Sinai.

Exodus connects the trumpet and smoking mountain with the people's fear and request that Moses speak instead of God, lest they die. Hebrews describes hearers begging for no further word. The respective sound/seeing language and the shortened request remain as printed.

The Exodus boundary rule forbids touching the mountain and includes beast or person under death by stoning or a dart. Hebrews cites the animal-touching and stoning part in explaining the hearers' fear. The other penalty wording and the broader boundary details are not silently removed from Exodus.

Deuteronomy's first-person fear because of the Lord's wrath provides a qualified comparison with Moses' terror in Hebrews. Deuteronomy places the fear in pleading over the people's sins; it does not print trembling or independently narrate exactly the mountain sight named here. The similar fear language is not called an identical full quotation.

Heavenly Jerusalem corresponds to Galatians' Jerusalem above. Galatians describes that Jerusalem as free and our mother; Hebrews names the living God's city, Mount Zion and the angelic festive gathering. The city language is related without inserting the different maternal or angelic details into the other unit.

Both use heavenly registration language: firstborn ones enrolled in the heavens in Hebrews, and names written in the heavens in Luke. Luke's address to the rejoicing messengers does not identify every member of the assembly or define the perfected righteous spirits; its submitting spirits are not equated with that latter group.

Both explicitly call Jesus or the previously described Christ mediator of a new covenant. Hebrews9 explains the death, redemption and promised eternal inheritance; Hebrews12 places Jesus with the sprinkled-blood comparison. Those additional predicates are not exchanged as identical clauses.

Genesis identifies Abel as Cain's brother and describes his blood's voice crying to God from the earth. Hebrews' sprinkled blood speaks better than Abel. This connects the unusual blood-and-speaking imagery without turning Genesis' cry into an unprinted explicit prayer for revenge or resolving every sense of better.

Both arguments compare earlier disobedience receiving recompense with the danger of refusing the present message. Hebrews2 contrasts the angel-mediated word with neglect of the Lord-announced salvation; Hebrews12 contrasts instruction on earth with turning from the One from the heavens. The particular agency descriptions are not collapsed.

Both announce another shaking of heaven and earth. Haggai names the Lord Almighty and also sea and dry land, with heaven first; Hebrews says not only earth but also heaven after recalling the former shaking. The order, scope and yet-once-more wording retain their differences.

The quoted yet once more is immediately supplied by the preceding promise to shake earth and heaven. This unit then explains it through removal of made things and what remains unshaken. The connection identifies the quotation being interpreted rather than claiming Haggai itself prints the whole removal explanation.

Both describe receiving or being given the kingdom. Luke says the Father was pleased to give the little flock the kingdom; Hebrews describes receiving an unshakable kingdom and responding with gratitude and acceptable service. The fear, gratitude and unshakable formulations remain distinct.

The consuming-fire statement about God corresponds directly to Deuteronomy's Lord-your-God consuming fire. Deuteronomy also says a jealous God in a covenant/idolatry warning; Hebrews uses the statement to ground reverent service. The different pronouns and additional title are retained.

Both explicitly urge brotherly love. Romans develops it through tender devotion to one another and taking the lead in honor; Hebrews gives the concise appeal that it remain. The fuller actions in Romans are related instructions, not additional words of this Hebrews unit.

Genesis explicitly calls the visitors two angels and narrates Lot urging them into his house, lodging and feeding them. This is a concrete hospitality-to-angels counterpart to Hebrews' encouragement. Genesis does not state when Lot recognized their nature, and Hebrews does not identify Lot by name or make this its only possible example.

Both call attention to imprisoned people: Matthew's judgment scene includes coming to the speaker in prison, while Hebrews urges remembrance as fellow prisoners and solidarity with the mistreated as people in a body. The visit and shared-vulnerability instructions are not identical clauses or a claim that all prisoners have the same identity.

Both connect sexual conduct with divine judgment or avenging. Thessalonians calls for abstention from sexual immorality and sanctification and honor, with the Lord an avenger of the specified wrongs; Hebrews names an honored marriage and undefiled bed, then God's judgment of sexually immoral people and adulterers. Vessel is left as printed, without deciding its debated referent from this link.

Both pair contentment with a warning about the love of money. Timothy develops food and coverings, the wish to become rich and wandering from the faith; Hebrews urges contentment with what is present and grounds it in God's nonabandonment promise. The specific harms and promise remain their own clauses.

The promise of not forsaking corresponds to the Lord's assurance to Joshua. Joshua also says not disregard you and speaks of presence as with Moses, opposition and apportioning land; Hebrews says not leave or forsake in its contentment appeal. The wording and new application are distinguished without transferring Joshua's land or military promises to every reader.

The Lord-as-helper and refusal-to-fear-human-action saying corresponds to Psalms117:6. Hebrews presents the human-action clause as a question and introduces confident communal speech; the Psalm prints what a man will do to me after I will not fear. The actual formulations and Greek-based Psalm numbering are kept.

Both direct attention to leaders whose ministry concerns the community. Thessalonians asks recognition and high regard in love for people who labor, lead and admonish; Hebrews asks remembrance of people who spoke God's word and imitation of their faith after considering their way of life's outcome. It does not say these are the same named leaders or specify an identical office structure.

Hebrews1's cited address says Thou art the same and Thy years will not fail, while13:8 explicitly names Jesus Christ as the same yesterday, today and for the ages. The earlier remaining/changing contrast and the later temporal formulation provide an internal enduring-sameness connection without supplying a complete account of every implication of that sameness.

Colossians questions submission to handling, tasting and touching decrees, identifies human teachings and says their severe bodily practices have no value against fleshly indulgence. Hebrews likewise warns about teachings and says the foods have not benefited their adherents, contrasting them with grace strengthening the heart. The opponents and the precise rules are not assumed to be identical.

Leviticus distinguishes offerings priests may eat from sin offerings whose blood enters the Tent of Testimony and which must not be eaten. This supplies a specific sacrificial-eating restriction beside Hebrews' altar and the tent servants' lack of eating rights. It is ritual background, not a complete definition of our altar or an identification of a present-day religious group.

Leviticus specifies carrying the calf and male young goat for sin outside the camp and burning their bodies after their blood was brought into the holy place. Hebrews summarizes that same blood-inside/bodies-burned-outside rule, naming the high priest. The precise animals and washing requirements remain in their own Levitical context.

John records Jesus going out to the Skull place and being crucified at a place near the city. This supplies a concrete death-scene counterpart to Hebrews' suffering outside the gate. John names no gate in this range and does not print Hebrews' explanation about sanctifying the people through His own blood.

The earlier example values the reproach of Christ above Egypt's treasures and leaves Egypt by faith. Hebrews13 similarly joins going out with bearing His reproach. This is an internal reproach-and-departure comparison across different settings, not a claim that the earlier departure was outside Jerusalem or the same journey as the readers' appeal.

The earlier faith examples desire a heavenly homeland and have a city prepared by God; the closing appeal says there is no lasting city here and seeks the one to come. This is an internal future-city theme, without identifying an earthly address or adding an unprinted timetable.

Both explicitly call for a sacrifice of praise to God. The Psalm also names paying vows to the Most High; Hebrews names offering continually through Him and defines praise as the fruit of confessing lips. The extra details are not represented as a single identical quotation.

Hosea's return-with-words appeal ends with repaying the fruit of our lips. Hebrews uses the same fruit-of-lips image to explain continual praise confessing God's name through Him. Hosea's repentance appeal and Hebrews' mediating and praise wording remain distinct; no other edition's calves wording is inserted.

Philippians describes the supplied gift received through Epaphroditus as an acceptable sacrifice well pleasing to God. Hebrews likewise calls doing good and sharing sacrifices with which God is pleased. The particular gift and messenger illustrate that sacrificial description without being identified as the transaction in Hebrews.

Both concern care and oversight of the community. Hebrews addresses those who should obey and yield to leaders who watch and must give account; Peter addresses elders who should shepherd willingly and become examples rather than lord it over the flock. Their respective addressees, responsibilities and authority language remain distinct.

The request pray for us corresponds to Thessalonians' brothers, pray also for us. Hebrews additionally gives a conviction about good conscience and desired good conduct. The shared appeal does not identify the unnamed Hebrews writer or make the added conscience claim part of Thessalonians' short request.

Both connect a desired reunion with the recipients' prayers. In Hebrews do this continues the preceding pray-for-us request so the writer may be restored sooner; Philemon asks lodging and hopes to be graciously given to the recipient through prayers. Neither is treated as an already fulfilled release or proof of shared authorship or itinerary.

Ezekiel groups one shepherd, the named servant David as ruler and an everlasting covenant of peace. Hebrews groups the God of peace, the great shepherd Jesus and an eternal covenant. The cluster supplies a qualified scriptural thematic counterpart; Ezekiel does not here name Jesus, describe His resurrection or covenant blood, or equate the two printed personal names as a biographical identity.

Both attribute work pleasing to God to God's activity in people. Philippians names God working in you to will and work for His good pleasure; Hebrews continues the God-of-peace blessing by asking Him to equip you and work in us through Jesus Christ. The you/us pronouns, equipment request and mediation wording are preserved.

Both closing descriptions speak of writing briefly and encouragement or exhortation. Peter explicitly names Silvanus and testimony to true grace; Hebrews urges bearing with its word of encouragement. The common letter description does not supply a shared writer, recipient or Silvanus's unprinted role in Hebrews.

Both travel notices associate Timothy with a hoped-for visit and timing. Philippians hopes to send Timothy and for the writer also to come; Hebrews reports Timothy released and conditionally proposes seeing the recipients with him if he comes soon. The notices do not establish the same journey, release circumstances or the unnamed Hebrews writer's identity.

Both join an instruction to give greetings with greetings sent by a group. Hebrews names leaders, saints and those from Italy; Romans names one another with a holy kiss and all the Churches of Christ. From Italy is preserved and does not itself locate the Hebrews writer in Italy or identify the greeting group as a named Roman congregation.

The short closing grace wish corresponds to Titus's grace be with all of you. Hebrews prints grace be with you all, while Titus precedes it with personal greetings. No extra title, Amen or identity of writer is supplied to the concise Hebrews conclusion.
